title: Mahavira Makes Numbers Practical
subtitle: How a Jain Scholar Turned Subtle Numbers into Everyday Tools
region: Rashtrakuta-Ganga Jain scholarly sphere of Karnataka
moral: Clear numbers can outlive the courts that nurtured them.

sources.citation: Mahaviracharya, Ganita Sara Sangraha, c. 9th century
sources.note: Primary mathematical treatise covering arithmetic, fractions, mensuration, series and combinations.

sources.citation: T.A. Sarasvati Amma, Geometry in Ancient and Medieval India (1979); Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009)
sources.note: Modern history of Indian mathematics and Mahavira's place in it.

sources.citation: George Gheverghese Joseph, The Crest of the Peacock (3rd ed., 2011)
sources.note: Accessible synthesis of Indian mathematical traditions.

panels.shot: low-angle mid-wide of a scholar in a pillared Jain temple hall, palm-leaf manuscript in hand, numbers and geometric forms sketched on the floor around him

dialogue.text: In 9th‑century Karnataka, as kings fought for land, a Jain mathematician named Mahāvīrācārya quietly forged a handbook that made subtle numbers serve merchants, builders and thinkers for a thousand years.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye wide over the Deccan landscape, showing hilltop Jain temples and distant fortified cities under a hazy sky

dialogue.text: Around 850 CE, the Deccan shook under Rashtrakuta and Ganga rivalries, yet between their courts Jain scholars in Karnataka moved freely, carrying not swords but palm leaves filled with numbers.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Mahāvīrācārya seated cross-legged in a quiet Jain temple cloister, manuscripts spread before him

dialogue.text: Mahāvīrācārya was a Jain scholar, likely under King Amoghavarsha’s Rashtrakuta shadow, drawing on older works like Āryabhaṭa and Bhāskara I, yet restless to tighten and arrange their scattered rules.

panels.shot: medium close-up on Mahāvīrācārya’s hands as he copies and annotates an older manuscript

dialogue.text: The older Sanskrit verses gave rules for sines, circles, progressions and place‑value. Mahāvīra’s question was sharp: how can this living stream of ganita be organised so anyone trained may drink from it?

panels.shot: wide interior shot of a Jain temple school, with young students, an abacus-like counting board, and merchants observing

dialogue.text: In Karnataka’s Jain schools, commerce pressed on theory. Grain dealers, land stewards and temple builders needed clear methods for shares, depths, volumes, interest and partitions, not only sky‑circles and stars.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on Mahāvīrācārya’s face, eyes reflecting rows of numbers and geometric figures

dialogue.text: Mahāvīrācārya’s answer took the form of a single text in simple metrical Sanskrit, the Gaṇita‑Sāra‑Saṅgraha—‘Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics’—that marched from basic numeration through geometry to combinations.

panels.shot: tabletop overhead shot of a palm-leaf colophon page being inscribed with the title and chapter divisions

dialogue.text: He set his work in nine chapters: on numbers, the basic operations, fractions, mixed fractions, series, geometry and mensuration, shadows, combinations and permutations, and a closing garland of practical tasks.

panels.shot: medium shot of Mahāvīrācārya teaching two students using a dust board, writing 0 within a larger numeral

dialogue.text: Older Indian texts had already used empty places and a dot for zero; Mahāvīra firmly gave zero its seat among numbers, treating it in addition, subtraction, multiplication and division like any other digit.

panels.shot: close-up of the dust board showing Mahāvīrācārya writing a small circle and demonstrating an operation

dialogue.speaker: mahaviracharya
dialogue.text: Where nothing is, we place a sign; where nothing stands, the count still flows.

panels.shot: medium-wide of Mahāvīrācārya guiding a student through a fraction problem with a merchant listening nearby

dialogue.text: He worked out clear rules for fractions—reducing, comparing, adding and subtracting shares—framing them in verses about dividing fields, barrels of ghee, and partnership profits so that reciters could remember and apply.

panels.shot: wide shot of a courtyard where builders measure a rectangular foundation while Mahāvīrācārya watches

dialogue.text: The Gaṇita‑Sāra‑Saṅgraha gathered area and volume rules for rectangles, triangles, circles, heaps and tanks, echoing older śulba and astronomical texts but polishing them into one ready handbook for craftsmen and scribes.

panels.shot: medium shot of Mahāvīrācārya drawing a circle and inscribing a polygon inside it on a board

dialogue.text: Geometry in his verse dealt with chords, circles and polygons in the practical Indian fashion—rules for circumferences, chord lengths and areas—without proof diagrams, yet precise enough for architecture and land survey.

panels.shot: close-up of a palm-leaf where a problem verse about combinations is being written, showing arrangements of syllables as tiny marks

dialogue.text: Most striking were his chapters on combinations and permutations—counting ways to arrange and choose objects—building on a long Indian taste for prosody and arrangements, now turned into general rules for ordered selections.

panels.shot: medium shot of Mahāvīrācārya explaining a combinations problem about garlands or jewels to a noble patron

dialogue.speaker: mahaviracharya
dialogue.text: Change the order, and the count grows. Fix the order, and the count falls.

panels.shot: wide shot of a dim hall where Mahāvīrācārya dictates while a group of scribes copy his text onto fresh palm leaves

dialogue.text: He cast his rules as terse verses easy to chant, then oversaw copies for far monasteries and schools, turning his own memory into a thing that could travel, be recited, checked and corrected.

panels.shot: montage-like wide showing different users: a merchant tallying, a land surveyor, a temple accountant, all with manuscripts referencing similar diagrams

dialogue.text: Over time, his compendium joined the working library of merchants, accountants, land‑record keepers and teachers, who found in it a consistent path from simple counting into shares, interest, measures and rarer puzzles.

panels.shot: medium shot of a later medieval mathematician reading Mahāvīrācārya’s text alongside a newer manuscript, in a different script

dialogue.text: Later mathematicians like Bhāskara II met Mahāvīra as one voice among many, sometimes praising, sometimes correcting his rules, yet still copying his problems and structure into their own broader treasuries of ganita.

panels.shot: wide shot of Shravanabelagola hill with a Jain temple, juxtaposed with faint overlay of numerical verses in the sky

dialogue.text: The same Jain networks that carved stone colossi at places like Śravaṇabelagola also quietly fostered such mathematical texts, tying the stillness of their hills to the restless movement of accounts and measures.

panels.shot: slow pull-back from a close-up of the Gaṇita-Sāra-Saṅgraha manuscript to a shelf of many later works, while faint sounds of old courts fade

dialogue.text: Mahāvīrācārya did not invent zero or algebra, but by gathering old currents into one ordered stream, he made numbers clear enough to outlast the Rashtrakuta courts that once sheltered his quiet labour.
